newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: No major purchase for ABN AMRO after sale.
newsitem.headline: No major purchase for ABN AMRO after sale.

text.p: Dutch financial titan ABN AMRO said on Saturday the sale of investment banking arm MeesPierson to Dutch-Belgian group Fortis would end an overlap in its activities but ruled out using the proceeds to fund a big acquisition.
"There was a gradual process in the minds of the management that there was an overlap which gave little room for MeesPierson to develop," ABN AMRO spokesman Jules Prast told Reuters.
"We are convinced this is the best possible solution."
ABN AMRO and Fortis announced late on Friday that a letter of intent to sell MeesPierson had been signed and that the deal, widely expected by analysts, would be finalised in two months.

No financial details were given but analysts reckon the sale of the unit, which has 4,000 staff worldwide and assets of over 50 billion guilders ($29 billion) in cash and securities under management, could generate up to 2.5 billion guilders.

"Noone should think ABN AMRO is on the verge of a major change in its expansion philosophy. We will still have an expansion philisophy based on autonomous growth and sometimes smaller acquisitions," he said.
Analysts have suggested the company may focus on expanding its loan book in South East Asia.
Prast said it would be wrong to argue the bank would now want to use the money from the sale to fund a large purchase.
"That is not going to happen," he said, adding that in any case the group already had large shareholder funds and cash flow making such a purchase possible, should it have wanted.

Rumours of a potential spin-off of MeesPierson have been circulating since 1992 when ABN AMRO bought British securities house Hoare Govett and began expanding into investment banking. For this reason, Prast said the divestment did not leave ABN AMRO without a presence in this lucrative market.

"MeesPierson was an independently managed bank. The sale will still leave ABN AMRO with Hoare Govett which has a network of over 5,000 people in around 40 countries. We still have a complete investment banking arm," he said.
Friday's announcement ended a week of mounting speculation over the fate of MeesPierson, although Fortis had emerged as the main buyer candidate and the deal is regarded a good fit.

Analysts have said Fortis is under-developed in the field of investment and private banking and the incorporation of MeesPierson would enhance its existing retail banking activities and increase its earnings per share.
"It's a great addition to existing Fortis activities. It's complementary and there's no real overlap," Fortis spokeswoman Saskia van Opijnen said on Saturday.

She said the acquisition would probably be financed through a re-allocation of resources and possible increase in leverage. Fortis' debt to equity ratio was fairly low, she said. Details were still being worked out.
Both groups now have around two months to complete the process of due dilligance and formulate a joint business plan.

MeesPierson was formed in 1993 through a merger of Mees & Hope and Pierson, Heldring & Pierson, the Dutch investment bank units of Algemene Bank Nederland (ABN) and Amsterdam-Rotterdam Bank (AMRO), which themselves merged in 1991 to form ABN AMRO.
